title: Group Supervision November 11, 2026
author: Unlocked Graduates
summary: This piece describes a short, structured peer-support practice that the Unlocked Graduates programme runs for prison officers and argues that any team can adopt it. The central claim is that small, unresolved workplace problems, too minor for a line manager but corrosive over time, deserve a regular and solution-focused forum. The author sets out the model's purpose, its three roles of facilitator, presenter and group member, and the discipline of staying in role. The move is to present a low-cost practice as scalable, backed by research on a comparable social care model and by the programme's own survey figures. It also distinguishes the practice from clinical staff support and from reflective practice. The piece closes with the pitfalls each role should avoid.
points: Group supervision is a solution-focused peer tool for problems with no obvious answer.
It targets the small frustrations that never reach a line manager but wear teams down.
Three roles (facilitator, presenter, group member) keep sessions short, inclusive and focused.
It differs from reflective practice by centring a specific workplace challenge and actions.
Survey results and retention figures are offered as evidence that the model works.
quotes: The Unlocked group supervision model is a solution-focused peer support tool. It helps participants, the graduates on our two-year programme, solve the knotty problems they meet as prison officers on the landings, and builds collaborative problem solving at work.
Group supervision works best for problems with no obvious answer. A participant might disagree with a decision their line manager made, and feel it is really not working.
These are the problems that may never feel big enough to take up line management time, but cause daily frustration, low-level grumbling and, in the end, less fulfilment at work.
The structure is designed to keep sessions short and impactful. It draws contributions from the whole group, so there are multiple perspectives.

Before group supervision becomes an embedded practice, sticking to the structure can feel awkward for everyone. It is important to hold to it, because it keeps the conversation solution-focused and constructive.

Facilitators: holding back from contributing can be hard, particularly when the answer seems obvious. But staying in role keeps the space inclusive, focused and time-bound, and lets the group find solutions for itself.
Presenters: prepare well. Describe the situation fully and know what you want from the group.
